sections.title: Midpoints and Perpendicular Bisectors of Chords
Distance of Chords from the Centre

slides.title: What Exactly Is a Circle
slides.kicker: One rule, endless points, perfect roundness.
bullets: A circle is the set of all points on a plane that are equidistant from one given point on that plane.
That given point is the centre, and the distance from the centre to any point on the circle is the radius.
In the book's figure, every point at distance AB from the centre A forms the circle with centre A and radius AB.
slides.note: Same distance from one point, that is the whole secret.

slides.title: Locus, a Useful Word
slides.kicker: Math has a neat word for rule-following points.
bullets: The set of all points that satisfy a given condition is called the locus of points satisfying that condition.
So a circle can be described as the locus of points that are equidistant from a given point.
Think of it as a membership rule: every point that obeys the rule joins the locus, and no other point gets in.
slides.note: Locus is a fancy address book for points.

slides.title: Chords and Diameters
slides.kicker: Join two circle points and watch what happens.
bullets: Let B and C be two points on a circle; the line segment BC joining them is called a chord of the circle.
A chord that passes through the centre of the circle gets a special name, the diameter.
In a circle of radius 5 units, the chord through the centre, the diameter, has length 10 units.
slides.note: A diameter is a chord with a VIP pass through the centre.

slides.title: Angle a Chord Subtends
slides.kicker: The chord opens an angle at the centre.
bullets: Join the ends of chord BC to the centre A and the angle BAC appears.
The book calls angle BAC the angle subtended by the chord BC at the centre.
Subtended simply names the angle that the chord opens up when you look at it from that point.

items: Take a chord BC on the circle
Join B and C to the centre A
Angle BAC is the angle subtended at the centre

slides.note: Subtended = the angle the chord throws open at a point.

slides.title: The Wheel That Hides Its Turn
slides.kicker: Spin it how you like, it looks the same.
bullets: Watch a wheel of a vehicle touch the ground, then look again later; you can never tell if the touching point is the same point.
A rotating wheel looks the same at all times, so we say the circle has complete rotational symmetry.
Rotate a circle by any angle at all and it looks exactly the same as before the turn.
slides.note: Wheels are the masters of disguise.

slides.title: Fold Paper, Find a Diameter
slides.kicker: One fold and symmetry becomes visible.
bullets: Cut a paper circle and fold it so that the two boundaries overlap; the crease is a line of reflection symmetry.
Ask whether the crease passes through the centre: it does, so the crease is a diameter of the circle.
Every diameter you can draw is a line of reflection symmetry of the circle.
slides.note: Folding is honest work; the crease never lies.

slides.title: Two Kinds of Symmetry
slides.kicker: Rotating and folding, both leave it unchanged.
bullets: In rotational symmetry you turn the figure about its centre and it matches itself again.
In reflection symmetry you fold along a line and the two halves cover each other exactly.
For the circle the rotation angle can be anything, and every diameter works as the folding line.
slides.note: The circle wins both symmetry contests.

slides.title: Think and Reflect Corner
slides.kicker: The book leaves juicy puzzles here.
bullets: Puzzle one: a circle has radius 5 units; the book asks for the length of the longest chord, and whether a smallest chord exists.
Puzzle two: points at a given distance from a given point form a circle; what is the locus equidistant from two given points?
The hint: equidistant points lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB, and we must also show all points on it are equidistant.
slides.note: Longest chord here is the diameter: 10 units.

slides.title: Circles Through Two Points
slides.kicker: How many circles can pass through A and B?
bullets: The chapter asks: given two points A and B on a plane, how many circles pass through both of them?
If a circle passes through A and B with centre O, then the lengths OA and OB must be equal.
Every point equidistant from A and B can serve as the centre of a circle passing through A and B.

items: Pick a point equidistant from A and B
Draw the circle through A and B

slides.note: Pick a new centre, get a brand new circle.

slides.title: Centre Lives on the Bisector
slides.kicker: The perpendicular bisector collects every centre.
bullets: The perpendicular bisector of segment AB is the locus of points equidistant from A and B.
Every point on it is equidistant from A and B, and every point equidistant from A and B lies on it.
So the centres of all circles through A and B lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB.

items: A circle through A and B needs OA = OB
Equidistant points form the perpendicular bisector
So all such centres sit on that line

slides.note: One line holds the whole family of centres.

slides.title: The Smallest Circle Through Two
slides.kicker: Meet the circle where AB is the diameter.
bullets: Take the midpoint of segment AB as centre; a circle passing through A and B can be drawn with it.
Its radius is half the length of AB, and AB is a diameter of this circle.
The book's figure shows circles with centres K, J and L, all passing through the same two points C and D.
slides.note: Hug the segment tightly and you get the tiniest one.

slides.title: Now Try Three Points
slides.kicker: The book's natural next question.
bullets: It is natural to ask: how many circles can you draw through three distinct points A, B and C on a plane?
Is there always at least one such circle? The chapter builds towards answering exactly this.
Later the book uses Theorem 1: when A, B, C are noncollinear points, there is a circle passing through all three.
slides.note: Hold that thought till the concyclicity section.

slides.title: Centre to Chord Midpoint
slides.kicker: Draw one line and something special happens.
bullets: The book asks: what do we get when we draw a segment from the centre of a circle to the midpoint of a chord?
Theorem 4 answers: the line joining the centre of a circle and the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord.
So centre plus midpoint always gives a perfect right angle at the chord.
slides.note: Centre to midpoint always lands at 90 degrees.

slides.title: Why Theorem 4 Is True
slides.kicker: Isosceles triangle plus congruence does the job.
bullets: Triangle CAB is isosceles because CA and CB are both radii, so CA equals CB and angle A equals angle B.
M is the midpoint of AB, so AM equals BM; by the SAS congruence, triangle CMA is congruent to triangle CMB.
Then angle CMB equals angle CMA; together they make 180 degrees on the line AB, so each of them is 90 degrees.

items: AM = BM, M is the midpoint
Angles at M are 90 degrees each

slides.note: Two radii quietly built an isosceles triangle for us.

slides.title: The Converse: Theorem 5
slides.kicker: Flip the theorem, it still works.
bullets: Exercise Set 5.3 asks you to explain why the converse of Theorem 4 is true.
You are told that angle CMA and angle CMB are both 90 degrees, and you need to show that AM equals BM.
The result is Theorem 5: the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.
slides.note: Same picture, read backwards.

slides.title: Isosceles Triangle on a Circle
slides.kicker: An exercise that surprises many students.
bullets: Exercise Set 5.3 inscribes an isosceles triangle ABC in a circle, with AB equal to AC.
The task: show that the altitude drawn from A down to BC passes straight through the centre of the circle.
Reasoning path: with AB equal to AC the altitude is the perpendicular bisector of chord BC, and by Theorem 5 the centre lies on it.

items: AB = AC, isosceles on the circle
Altitude from A bisects chord BC
Centre lies on that perpendicular line

slides.note: The altitude is a secret centre detector.

slides.title: Paper Folding With Chords
slides.kicker: Crease a chord, then crease its bisector.
bullets: Fold a paper circle from the boundary inwards and open it: the crease is a chord of the circle.
Fold again so the two end points of the chord meet; the new crease runs along the perpendicular from the centre to the chord.
The chord gets bisected exactly where the two folds intersect.

items: Fold boundary inwards: a chord appears
Fold so the chord endpoints meet

slides.note: Your thumbs just demonstrated half of Theorem 5.

slides.title: Distance From Centre to Chord
slides.kicker: One measurement, clearly defined.
bullets: The distance from the centre to a chord means the distance from the centre to the midpoint of the chord.
That length is the length of the perpendicular from the centre to the chord, as the folding activity shows.
Draw another chord of the same length, join the centre to its midpoint, and compare the two measurements.
slides.note: Distance to a chord always means this perpendicular.

slides.title: The Tracing Paper Trick
slides.kicker: Rotate and equal chords swap places.
bullets: Draw the same circle on tracing paper, copy the chord and its perpendicular, then rotate the top paper.
The chord glides to a different position but keeps the same length, because rotating the circle about its centre does not change the circle.
After rotating, the perpendicular matches too, so equal chords appear to be equidistant from the centre.

items: Chord lands on a new equal chord

slides.note: Rotation is the circle's favourite magic trick.

slides.title: A Guess Is Not a Proof
slides.kicker: Many examples still need one reason.
bullets: The book warns: a statement may be true on a large number of examples and still not be true in general.
So the guess becomes Theorem 6, proved properly: chords of a circle having the same length are all at the same distance from the centre.
Setup: chords AB and FG have AB equal to FG, with midpoints E and H; the goal is to show CE equals CH.
From Theorem 5, CE and CH are the perpendiculars, so they are exactly the distances from the centre C to the chords.
slides.note: Examples suggest, proofs settle.

slides.title: What Is an Arc?
slides.kicker: Two points, one curved road.
bullets: An arc of a circle is a connected portion of the circle.
It is defined by two points on the circle, called the end points, and the curve connecting them along the circle's edge.
From A to B there are two ways to travel along the circle: one goes via point X and one goes via point Y.
slides.note: Two arcs share the same end points.

slides.title: Minor and Major Arcs
slides.kicker: Small road, big road, both from A to B.
bullets: The bigger of the two arcs between A and B is called the major arc, and the smaller one is the minor arc.
The minor arc AXB subtends the angle AOB at the centre, moving from OA to OB via X.
The major arc subtends the angle we get moving from OA to OB via Y, the bigger sweep.
If the angle at the centre is less than 180 degrees the arc is minor; if it is greater than 180 degrees it is major.
slides.note: Under 180 degrees at the centre means minor.

slides.title: Angle at Another Point C
slides.kicker: Move C around; the angle refuses to change.
bullets: The angle subtended by arc AXB at a point C on the circle outside the arc means the angle ACB.
Remarkably, this measure does not depend on which specific point C we pick, so long as C is on the circle and outside the arc.
Slide C along the circle and angle ACB stays the same, which feels almost like magic.

items: Pick any C on the circle outside it
Move C: the angle stays the same

slides.note: The arc sets the angle; the point hardly matters.

slides.title: Measure at P, Q and R
slides.kicker: An activity before the theorem.
bullets: Draw a circle with a chord AB and fix the arc AKB, with K a point between A and B on the circle.
Measure the angle the arc subtends at the centre, then at three points P, Q and R on the circle outside the arc.
The three angles at P, Q and R come out equal every time, for this arc and for any other arc you repeat with.

items: Fix chord AB and arc AKB
Measure the angle at centre O
Measure angles at P, Q, R

slides.note: Do it twice; the pattern will not blink.

slides.title: Theorem 9: Centre Doubles
slides.kicker: The headline result of this section.
bullets: Theorem 9: the angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle it subtends at a point on the circle outside the arc.
So if an arc makes 60 degrees at a point on the circle outside it, it makes 120 degrees at the centre.
This single rule powers the next section on concyclic points and cyclic quadrilaterals.

items: Angle at point P outside the arc

slides.note: Central angle is the double of the rim angle.

slides.title: Concyclic Points
slides.kicker: One circle, many members.
bullets: Points that lie on the same circle are called concyclic.
The book answers the question of when four points lie on one circle, and lets you explore five points, six points and beyond.
The whole question turns on the angles that one segment subtends at the other points.
slides.note: Concyclic is the guest list of one circle.

slides.title: Theorem 10: Equal Angles, One Circle
slides.kicker: Equal looks from C and D force a circle.
bullets: Theorem 10: if a segment AB subtends equal angles at points C and D on the same side of AB, the four points lie on a circle.
Both C and D must be off the line AB, and angle ACB equals angle ADB.
First move of the proof: A, B, C are noncollinear, so using Theorem 1 there is a circle passing through A, B, C.

items: AB with C and D on the same side
Draw the circle through A, B, C
Question: is D on it too?

slides.note: Equal viewing angles hint at a shared circle.

slides.title: Proof by Impossible Angle
slides.kicker: Push the wrong case until it contradicts.
bullets: Suppose D is not on the circle; then D is either inside or outside, and the line AD meets the circle at a point E.
C and E lie on the same segment of the arc formed by chord AB, so angle ACB equals angle AEB.
If D is outside, angle AEB is an exterior angle of triangle BED, so angle AEB is greater than angle ADB.
Chaining the equalities gives angle ACB greater than itself, impossible; the inside case fails the same way, so D is on the circle.

items: Assume D is off the circle
AD meets the circle at E
So D must be on the circle

slides.note: Contradiction is the bouncer at this door.

slides.title: Cyclic Quadrilaterals
slides.kicker: A 4-gon that lives on a circle.
bullets: When the vertices of a quadrilateral, which we also call a 4-gon, are concyclic, the quadrilateral is called a cyclic quadrilateral.
All four corners sit on one circle, which is a very special and useful situation.
The circle has a centre O, and the arcs between the vertices subtend angles at the opposite corners.
slides.note: Four corners, one circle, zero leftovers.

slides.title: Theorem 11: Opposites Make 180
slides.kicker: The classic cyclic quadrilateral result.
bullets: Theorem 11: the sum of two opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral is 180 degrees.
For a cyclic 4-gon ABCD on a circle with centre O, the claim is that angle BAD plus angle BCD equals 180 degrees.
Idea: arc BCD subtends angle BAD at A and arc BAD subtends angle BCD at C; the two arcs together make the whole circle.
The two central angles add to 360 degrees; by Theorem 9 each inscribed angle is half of its central angle, so the pair sums to 180 degrees.
slides.note: Opposite corners of a cyclic 4-gon always share 180.

flashcards.front: What is a circle, in one line?
flashcards.back: The set of all points on a plane that are equidistant from a given point on that plane; that point is the centre.

flashcards.front: What does the word locus mean?
flashcards.back: The set of all points that satisfy a given condition; a circle is the locus of points equidistant from a given point.

flashcards.front: What are a chord and a diameter?
flashcards.back: A chord is a segment joining two points of the circle; a diameter is a chord that passes through the centre.

flashcards.front: What is the radius of a circle?
flashcards.back: The distance from the centre to any point on the circle; every point at that distance from the centre lies on it.

flashcards.front: What is complete rotational symmetry?
flashcards.back: The figure looks exactly the same after a rotation by any angle; the spinning wheel of a vehicle is the book's example.

flashcards.front: How do you find a reflection line of a paper circle?
flashcards.back: Fold it so the two boundaries overlap; the crease is the line, it passes through the centre, so it is a diameter.

flashcards.front: Which lines are lines of reflection symmetry of a circle?
flashcards.back: All diameters of the circle; every one of them is a fold line that makes the halves overlap.

flashcards.front: What is the locus of points equidistant from two given points?
flashcards.back: The perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them; every point on it is equidistant, and every equidistant point is on it.

flashcards.front: How many circles pass through two given points?
flashcards.back: Infinitely many; every point equidistant from the two points can be the centre of one such circle.

flashcards.front: Where do the centres of all circles through A and B lie?
flashcards.back: On the perpendicular bisector of AB, because each centre must be equidistant from A and B.

flashcards.front: Describe the smallest circle through two points A and B.
flashcards.back: Its centre is the midpoint of AB, its radius is half the length of AB, and AB is a diameter.

flashcards.front: What question does the book raise about three points?
flashcards.back: How many circles pass through three distinct points A, B, C; later, noncollinear triples always get a circle by Theorem 1.

flashcards.front: State Theorem 4 about chords.
flashcards.back: The line joining the centre of a circle and the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord.

flashcards.front: State Theorem 5, the converse of Theorem 4.
flashcards.back: The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.

flashcards.front: Why is triangle CAB isosceles in the proof of Theorem 4?
flashcards.back: C is the centre and A, B are points on the circle, so CA and CB are both radii and hence equal.

flashcards.front: Which congruence proves triangles CMA and CMB congruent?
flashcards.back: SAS, using CA equals CB, equal base angles at A and B, and AM equals BM because M is the midpoint of AB.

flashcards.front: What does the second fold in the chord activity give?
flashcards.back: A crease along the perpendicular from the centre to the chord; the chord is bisected where the two creases meet.

flashcards.front: How is the distance from the centre to a chord measured?
flashcards.back: As the length of the perpendicular from the centre to the chord, that is, the centre to midpoint distance.

flashcards.front: State Theorem 6.
flashcards.back: Chords of a circle having the same length are all at the same distance from the centre of the circle.

flashcards.front: Why did the book prove Theorem 6 after the tracing paper test?
flashcards.back: Many examples suggest a rule but do not prove it; a statement true in many cases can still fail in general.

flashcards.front: What is an arc of a circle?
flashcards.back: A connected portion of the circle, fixed by two end points and the curve joining them along the circle's edge.

flashcards.front: When is an arc minor and when is it major?
flashcards.back: The smaller of the two arcs between two points is minor, the bigger is major; central angle under 180 degrees means minor.

flashcards.front: What is the angle subtended by arc AXB at a point C outside it?
flashcards.back: The angle ACB; its measure is the same no matter which point C on the circle outside the arc you choose.

flashcards.front: State Theorem 9.
flashcards.back: The angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle it subtends at a point on the circle outside the arc.

flashcards.front: What does concyclic mean?
flashcards.back: Points are concyclic when they all lie on the same circle.

flashcards.front: State Theorem 10.
flashcards.back: If a segment AB subtends equal angles at two points C, D on the same side of AB, then A, B, C, D lie on one circle.

flashcards.front: What is a cyclic quadrilateral?
flashcards.back: A quadrilateral, also called a 4-gon, whose vertices are concyclic, meaning all four lie on one circle.

flashcards.front: State Theorem 11.
flashcards.back: The sum of two opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral is 180 degrees.

quiz.q: A circle is the set of all points on a plane that are ____ from a given point.
options: on the boundary of a square
quiz.why: The book defines the circle by equal distance from the centre point.

quiz.q: In the book's figure, the angle subtended by chord BC at the centre A is:
quiz.why: Joining B and C to the centre A opens angle BAC at the centre.

quiz.q: A chord that passes through the centre of a circle is called a:
quiz.why: The book names the chord through the centre the diameter.

quiz.q: A circle has radius 5 units. The chord through its centre has length:
quiz.why: That chord is the diameter, made of two radii, so 2 times 5 equals 10.

quiz.q: Rotate a circle by any angle and it looks exactly the same. This property is called:
quiz.why: The wheel example shows the circle looks the same at all times while rotating.

quiz.q: Fold a paper circle so the boundaries overlap. The crease you see is:
quiz.why: The fold line passes through the centre, so it is a diameter.

quiz.q: How many lines of reflection symmetry does a circle have?
quiz.why: All diameters are lines of reflection symmetry of the circle.

quiz.q: The locus of points equidistant from two given points A and B is:
options: a circle through A and B
quiz.why: The Think and Reflect hint: equidistant points lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB.

quiz.q: How many circles pass through two given distinct points?
quiz.why: Every point on the perpendicular bisector can be the centre of one more circle.

quiz.q: AB is 8 cm. The circle with centre at the midpoint of AB that passes through A and B has radius:
quiz.why: Its radius is half the length of AB and AB is the diameter.

quiz.q: The centres of all circles passing through A and B must lie on:
quiz.why: A centre must satisfy OA equals OB, the defining property of the bisector.

quiz.q: As the centre moves farther from AB along the perpendicular bisector, the circle through A and B:
quiz.why: A farther centre gives a larger radius, so the arc through A and B flattens.

quiz.q: Theorem 4: the line joining the centre of a circle to the midpoint of a chord is ____ the chord.
quiz.why: Centre to midpoint always meets the chord at 90 degrees.

quiz.q: Theorem 5: the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord ____ the chord.
quiz.why: The converse result says the perpendicular cuts the chord into two equal parts.

quiz.q: In the proof of Theorem 4, why does angle CMB plus angle CMA equal 180 degrees?
options: Because they are angles on a line at M
Because CA and CB are radii
quiz.why: M sits on the line AB, so the two angles at M fill a straight angle.

quiz.q: An isosceles triangle ABC with AB equal to AC is inscribed in a circle. The altitude from A to BC:
options: passes through the centre of the circle
is a diameter of the circle
quiz.why: It is the perpendicular bisector of chord BC, and the centre lies on it by Theorem 5.

quiz.q: Theorem 6 says chords of a circle with the same length are:
options: all at the same distance from the centre
quiz.why: Equal length chords stand equally far from the centre.

quiz.q: In the paper folding activity, the chord gets bisected:
options: at the centre of the circle
quiz.why: The folds cross exactly at the midpoint of the chord.

quiz.q: For equal chords AB and FG with midpoints E and H, the book first notes that CE and CH are:
options: the perpendicular distances from centre C
quiz.why: By Theorem 5 they are the perpendiculars, hence the distances, from C to the chords.

quiz.q: Before proving Theorem 6, the book cautions that its rotation experiment:
options: is only an example, not a proof
quiz.why: True on a large number of examples does not mean true in general.

quiz.q: The smaller of the two arcs between two points on a circle is the:
quiz.why: Minor means smaller; the bigger one is the major arc.

quiz.q: An arc subtends 200 degrees at the centre of the circle. The arc is:
quiz.why: An angle at the centre greater than 180 degrees means a major arc.

quiz.q: Points P, Q, R lie on the circle outside arc AKB. The angles the arc subtends at them are:
quiz.why: The measure does not depend on which outside point you pick.

quiz.q: An arc subtends 60 degrees at a point on the circle outside it. At the centre it subtends:
quiz.why: Theorem 9: the angle at the centre is double the angle at the circle.

quiz.q: Points that lie on the same circle are called:
quiz.why: Concyclic literally means sitting on one common circle.

quiz.q: Theorem 10 concludes that A, B, C, D are concyclic when:
options: angle ACB equals angle ADB with C, D on the same side of AB
C and D are on opposite sides of AB
C and D lie on the line AB
quiz.why: Equal subtended angles from the same side force one circle.

quiz.q: In the proof of Theorem 10, if D were outside the circle, angle AEB is an exterior angle of triangle BED, so:
options: angle AEB is greater than angle ADB
angle AEB is smaller than angle ADB
quiz.why: The exterior angle exceeds the interior angle at D, which breaks the given equality.

quiz.q: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral and angle BAD is 110 degrees. Then angle BCD equals:
quiz.why: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180 degrees, so 180 minus 110 is 70.

examples.title: The Longest Chord
examples.problem: A circle has radius 5 units. What is the length of its longest chord, and what is that chord called?
steps: Recall from the definitions: a chord joins two points of the circle, and a chord passing through the centre is called a diameter.
The diameter runs from one side of the circle to the other through the centre, so its length is two radii: 2 x 5 = 10 units.
This is exactly the Think and Reflect question from the symmetries section, and the chord through the centre is the answer.
examples.answer: 10 units; the longest chord is the diameter.

examples.title: Distance Between Chord Midpoints
examples.problem: Two parallel chords of lengths 6 cm and 8 cm are on opposite sides of the centre of a circle. If the radius of the circle is 5 cm, find the distance between the midpoints of the chords.
steps: By Theorem 5, the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects it, so the halves of the chords are 3 cm and 4 cm.
Join the centre to one end of each chord; each joining segment is a radius of 5 cm, giving two right triangles at the midpoints.
Distance to the 6 cm chord: sqrt(5^2 - 3^2) = sqrt(25 - 9) = sqrt(16) = 4 cm.
Distance to the 8 cm chord: sqrt(5^2 - 4^2) = sqrt(25 - 16) = sqrt(9) = 3 cm.
The chords are on opposite sides of the centre, so the two distances add: 4 + 3 = 7 cm.
examples.answer: 7 cm between the midpoints of the two chords.

examples.title: Centre Angle From a Rim Angle
examples.problem: An arc of a circle subtends an angle of 60 degrees at a point on the circle outside the arc. What angle does the same arc subtend at the centre?
steps: Theorem 9 says the angle subtended by an arc at the centre is double the angle it subtends at a point on the circle outside the arc.
So the central angle is 2 x 60 = 120 degrees.
Check by reading backwards: the angle at the circle is half the central angle, and half of 120 is 60 degrees.

examples.title: Opposite Angles of a Cyclic 4-gon
examples.problem: ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral with angle BAD = 100 degrees and angle ABC = 75 degrees. Find angle BCD and angle ADC.
steps: Theorem 11: the sum of two opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral is 180 degrees.
Angle BCD is opposite to angle BAD, so angle BCD = 180 - 100 = 80 degrees.
Angle ADC is opposite to angle ABC, so angle ADC = 180 - 75 = 105 degrees.
Check: 100 + 80 = 180 and 75 + 105 = 180, so both opposite pairs sum correctly.
examples.answer: Angle BCD = 80 degrees and angle ADC = 105 degrees.

steps.label: Define the circle
steps.detail: Set of points equidistant from a centre; radius, chord, diameter.

steps.label: Spot the symmetry
steps.detail: Complete rotational symmetry; every diameter is a reflection line.

steps.label: Count the circles
steps.detail: Through two points: infinitely many, centres on the perpendicular bisector.

steps.label: Meet chord theorems
steps.detail: Theorem 4: centre to midpoint is perpendicular; Theorem 5: perpendicular bisects.

steps.label: Compare chord distances
steps.detail: Theorem 6: equal chords stand at equal distances from the centre.

steps.label: Ride the arcs
steps.detail: Minor and major arcs; the angles they subtend at the centre.

steps.label: Apply Theorem 9
steps.detail: Angle at the centre is double the angle at the circle.

steps.label: Test concyclicity
steps.detail: Theorem 10: equal angles on the same side put four points on one circle.

steps.label: Finish the 4-gon
steps.detail: Theorem 11: opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180 degrees.
